This report specifically addresses Objective 3, focusing on the integration of OTEC systems with floating oil and gas facilities. Background Funded by the Ocean Energy Safety Institute (OESI) 2.0, this research aligns with the institute's goals of enhancing U.S. energy security and promoting sustainable ocean energy production. OTEC is a renewable energy technology that leverages the temperature differential between warm surface seawater and cold deep seawater to generate electricity. This study assesses the feasibility of implementing OTEC systems offshore to reduce direct emissions from oil and gas operations and supply power for well monitoring systems. Approach The study builds on existing numerical models of closed-cycle OTEC plants, adapting them to include ammonia as a refrigerant and considering the largest commercially available cooling water intake pipes. The model allows users to input various parameters to simulate different OTEC plant configurations and calculate outputs such as gross and net power production, installation costs, and levelized cost of electricity (LCOE). OTEC and Oil and Gas Facility Collocation Concepts Three conceptual OTEC scenarios were developed: a small (100 kW) hull-integrated system, a medium (1.0 MW) add-on system, and a maximum (3.9 MW) add-on system. Each scenario was evaluated for its potential to offset power demand from offshore oil and gas operations. The study found that OTEC systems could provide significant power outputs, with the maximum scenario delivering an average net power of 3.9 MW. Some areas in the Gulf of America were identified as suitable locations for OTEC deployment due to favorable temperature gradients. iii OESI 2.0 M-1 T-1-P1.1 – Objective 3 Report April 2025 Interactive OTEC Location Model for the GOA As part of Objective 3, this study introduces a user-friendly interactive model designed to quickly assess the potential for OTEC power production in the Gulf of America (GOA). This tool, derived from the more complex numerical model developed in Objective 2, allows users to input key parameters such as location, cold-water intake depth, and pipe diameter to simulate different OTEC configurations. The interactive map features 60 potential locations in the Gulf, providing outputs that include power ratings, equipment and process parameters, and levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) calculations. Users can explore various scenarios by adjusting inputs like installation type and refrigerant choice, while the map displays essential attributes such as coordinates and water temperatures. This model serves as a valuable resource for stakeholders to evaluate hypothetical OTEC deployment possibilities, although it assumes new facility deployment rather than retrofitting existing ones. The model is published on Tableau Public and can be accessed by visiting: https://public.tableau.com/app/profile/otec.x.oil.and.gas.gulf.of.america.map/viz/ OTECxOilandGasInterface/Locations Conclusions and Key Insights The hypothetical OTEC visualization tool presented in this study has several limitations. The study assumes a scenario where OTEC systems are integrated into new facilities during the design phase, as retrofitting existing facilities is deemed cost-prohibitive.
